headline: Credicorp: ROE near 20% on 15% loan growth and a 6.9% margin, with extra provisions set aside for a “very strong” El Niño
takeaway: Net income rose 11% to S/1.93 billion, a 19.9% return on equity, as loans grew 14.8% and net interest income 17.7%. Provisions rose 37% because Credicorp now expects a very strong El Niño, and EPS of S/7.12 was slightly below forecasts, yet the shares rose 5.7% as asset quality kept improving.
results: Credicorp reported net income attributable to shareholders of S/1,929.4 million for the third quarter, up 11.0% from a year earlier and down 2.6% from the second quarter, giving a return on equity of 19.9%. Earnings per share were about S/7.12, slightly below the consensus of S/7.34.

Loans rose 14.8%, led by consumer and small-business lending at Banco de Crédito del Perú (BCP), then wholesale banking and Mibanco, where disbursements hit a record in September. Deposits rose 14.3%, with low-cost deposits at 73.2% of the total. Net interest income rose 17.7% and the net interest margin widened 0.36 points to 6.9% as asset yields rose to 8.8% and funding costs fell to 2.2%.

The non-performing loan ratio improved by 0.91 points to 3.9% and coverage rose to 120.9%, but provisions increased 37.4% and the cost of risk reached 2.0% after the bank raised its El Niño assessment to a “very strong” base case. Core income hit a record, up 18%, and efficiency improved to 45.4% over nine months.
mgmt: Management reaffirmed its 2026 return-on-equity guidance of about 19.5% and its medium-term target of about 22%. It said the quarter was driven by accelerating loan growth, healthy asset quality and diversified revenue, with continued investment in digital capabilities.

Credicorp’s innovation portfolio contributed 10.7% of risk-adjusted revenue, and Yape — its mobile payments and digital wallet app — contributed 9.8% as monetisation accelerated. The company also updated investors on its broader strategy and economic outlook for Peru and its other markets in Chile, Colombia, Bolivia and Panama.
view: Credicorp is the dominant financial group in Peru, and its results are increasingly a story about two businesses: a highly profitable traditional bank in BCP, and a fast-growing digital franchise built around Yape, which has become the default way Peruvians send money to each other. Yape contributing almost 10% of risk-adjusted revenue is the clearest sign yet that it is turning from a free payments app into a lender and marketplace that earns money from tens of millions of users who were previously outside the banking system.

The El Niño provisions are prudent rather than alarming. A strong El Niño brings floods to northern Peru that damage small businesses and agricultural borrowers — Mibanco’s core customers — and in 2017 and 2023 it hit loan quality hard. Building reserves ahead of the season, while NPLs are falling and coverage is rising, is the right sequence and explains why the market rewarded the quarter despite the slight EPS miss.

The broader risk is political. Peru has had repeated changes of president and went through general elections this year, and Credicorp’s valuation has historically swung with the political mood. Fundamentally, a bank earning close to 20% on equity with loan growth in the mid-teens and an improving digital mix trades at around 12 times earnings, a modest multiple for that profile. If the El Niño season proves manageable and Yape keeps compounding, the 22% medium-term ROE target looks credible.
watch: Watch the severity of El Niño and its effect on Mibanco’s loan quality, Yape’s revenue contribution and user monetisation, net interest margin as Peruvian rates move, and the policies of the new government.
